The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has launched, and it's glorious. But the real challenge isn't saving Hyrule as Link; it's finding a restock of the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
Restocks are rolling out — Target and Nintendo recently dropped fresh chances to grab the hard-to-find console — and with Nintendo promising more stock is on the way, I'm bringing you the latest stock updates.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . However, multiple retailers are prioritizing in-store restocks (Best Buy, Walmart, GameStop), so if you can, be sure to check your nearest locations.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years, and know how to secure in-demand items. Below are all the links you need, alongside live updates on Zelda Switch 2 restocks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
Nothing to report at present, Target has now returned to "sold out", though perhaps we'll see a third restock later today, meanwhile no signs of any stock at Walmart so the rumors are unfortunately looking increasingly unlikely. In-store remains your chance to find a Zelda Switch 2 , so if you live locally to a retailer, it's worth trying your luck. Meanwhile, my day is winding down, but I'll be handing over to a colleague shortly, to make sure you don't miss any restocks.
Quick update on the Target situation, I'm no longer seeing the "add to cart" button, but it does direct me to "show in-store stock" with at least one location popping up claiming to have stock nearby. It would seem all the online inventory has been snapped up, but I would still recommend checking for now, you could get lucky. And Target has restocked online twice now, could it go for a third?
I didn't see this one coming, but the "add to cart" button has just returned on Target, so get over there and see if you can secure a Zelda Switch 2 as it looks like stock is returning at the retailer!
All eyes are on Walmart at present, there are rumors flying around they will restock the Zelda Switch 2 today, but so far nothing. Remember, as I keep saying, there's no confirmation here, but restock rumors often prove to have some truth to them, so fingers firmly crossed the noise around Walmart amounts to a drop.
Well, after about an hour, I'm not seeing any signs of available stock at Target, even with a lot of refreshes, so I feel pretty confident saying the retailer is once again sold out . Hopefully you were able to grab one in this latest Zelda Switch 2 restock. If not, don't worry, I'm still here tracking stock levels across retailers. Remember, Walmart is rumored to drop next.
Target was the big one today, and after restocking in the very early morning hours, I wondered if that would be the retailer sold out again, but a second restock has appeared online. The console is going to sell out fast, so get over there, and even if you get a "sold out" message at first, keep trying, as more stock could appear.
No time for talking, the Zelda Switch 2 is IN STOCK at Target, go grab yours!!!
Last night after a busy day of restock tracking, I finally got to sink my teeth into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while I'm very early in my quest, my first impressions are that it's a glorious remake.
Our reviewer, Anthony Spadafora, had a similar experience, calling it "even better than my childhood memories." You can read his full Ocarina of Time review if you're looking to fill some time until we have more restock news to bring you.
Rumors have been flying around this week that Walmart could restock the Zelda Switch 2 from November 6 (aka today). This is based on an unverified leak of an internal document suggesting that the national retailer was gearing up for a restock. Again, this is all unconfirmed, but it's the retailer to watch right now, and it has already this week restocked in-store, so could an online drop follow today?
One of the big themes this week has been retailers opting for in-store restocks rather than dropping stock online.
I've just checked some local Target stores, and the retailer's online tracker is telling me there is Zelda Switch 2's available at nearby locations. However it's very limited ("only 1 left"), and these in-store stock trackers aren't always updated in realtime, so even if it tells you there's stock there's no guarantees.
Still, if you've got your heart set on securing a Zelda Switch 2, and have a Target store within reasonable distance (I wouldn't recommend a lengthy roadtrip), then getting down to your nearest location might be your best chance of getting one.
It looks like Target opted for a late-night online restock based on what I've seen on social media, so if you're still on the hunt for a Zelda Switch 2, that's the place to check now. But I'm seeing conflicting reports, with some users claiming that no stock was available, so I'll keep watching the retailer for signs of more stock.

The Trump administration quietly paid Elon Musk's SpaceX nearly $1.2 million in government contracts, despite previously characterizing the services as a “gift,” according to a report.
SpaceX was handed four contracts from March 2025 to June this year for Starlink services provided to the White House Communications Agency, a military unit responsible for managing secure comms for the president and executive officials, The Washington Post r eports.
The contracts amount to nearly $1.2 million, but in March last year, White House officials said that Starlink “donated” the service, per a New York Times report that has resurfaced.
“The gift had been vetted by the lawyer overseeing ethics issues in the White House Counsel’s Office,” the Times report stated, citing a White House official.
Three of the payments totalling $502,000 were reported last week by the legal advocacy group Democracy Defenders Fund. A fourth contract worth $686,000 was identified by the Post .
“I’m very concerned,” Virginia Canter, chief counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund, told the Post . “We worry about pay-to-play access and these kinds of transactional arrangements. When someone is given this access and subsequently given these government contracts, you have to wonder if these government contracts are in the best interest of the taxpayer.”
Starlink beams broadband internet to millions of customers in the U.S. using thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit. There were security concerns about the installation of Starlink’s services at the White House at the time.
Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the work was to “improve Wi-Fi connectivity on the complex” at the time.
The Independent has contacted the White House and the Pentagon, which paid for the services, and SpaceX for comment.
In its damning report, Democracy Defenders Fund alleged that in the 17 months since Musk publicly split with President Donald Trump, he has seen his net worth more than double, and his companies have netted at least $10 billion in new government contracts.
The revelation about the SpaceX contracts comes as Musk suffered a humiliating defeat in the midterms after he poured $500 million into Republican midterm campaigns to no avail.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk reacted on his X platform. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and ⁠is due to arrive in Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. local time (2:30 p.m. ET) for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.
Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.title_zh: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.content_orig:
China won’t be so quick to celebrate the stunning blue wave that washed over President Donald Trump this week.
American voters may have withdrawn the Republican mandate by giving Democrats the keys to Congress, but Trump can still direct his executive powers abroad, even as the opposition prepares to restrain him at home.
After a bruising midterm result for the U.S. president, a wounded Trump may seem like easy pickings for Chinese leader Xi Jinping , who will soon send negotiators to restart trade talks designed to neutralize America’s long-term tariff threat.
Xi had an understanding with Trump and knew what made him tick. But the political setback may make Trump much harder to predict .
Xi spent considerable resources on his rapprochement with Trump, including a state media campaign about Chinese resilience that stopped hostile economic acts by the United States and resulted in two glitzy state visits this year.
A promise to meet Trump at the APEC summit in southern China later this month, and again when Miami hosts the G20 meeting in December, has helped Xi build certainty into China’s relations with its top geopolitical rival.
Beijing may even go as far as to give Trump a foreign policy win at APEC by agreeing to a three-way meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in host city Shenzhen. Whether Xi makes any concrete commitments there is another question.
“Stability” has been the watchword in China for years, but it has extra weight this year after a campaign of purges swept up dozens of senior figures in elite Chinese politics and the military. Xi’s purges are about corruption in the Chinese Communist Party , but they’re also about loyalty—to him.
A recent gathering of the CCP’s Central Committee had the lowest attendance in over half a century, hinting at the scale of disciplinary action taken ahead of the party’s 21 st national congress in 12 months’ time, when Xi is widely expected to win an uncontested fourth 5-year term.
“Xi’s main political goal now is to secure another term at the 21st Party Congress. That requires not only a firm grip on power but also a case that his continued rule is legitimate and natural,” wrote Christopher Nye, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation think tank.
Xi used the latest gathering of party cadres “to resolve the problems of legitimacy created by the purge,” Nye wrote this week.
A fourth term could extend Xi’s rule over China to 20 years.
So, 2027 will be a delicate year for Xi. He’ll be wary of a Trump unleashed , who, despite being weakened domestically, could channel his energy into foreign policy matters, namely negotiations with China to extend or rip up the Busan truce that kept tariffs at a minimum in exchange for Chinese agricultural purchases and other key commitments.
“Beijing could conclude the election results mean Trump needs an economic agreement more than China does…. In that sense, Beijing could turn Trump’s political setback into a bargaining miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve,” said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
“If Beijing expects last night’s result to humble Trump, it is probably mistaken. He may have less room politically at home, but that could produce even bolder executive action abroad, including new pressure on Chinese companies, tighter economic-security measures and faster reshoring.
"Beijing should be careful about mistaking Trump’s political weakness for restraint in his China policy ."
Trump’s first presidency also began with personal diplomacy with China’s Xi before flattery gave way to full-blown systemic confrontation.
Trump hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in spring 2017 and Xi returned the favor in fall with a lavish state visit for Trump in Beijing. The two leaders appeared to agree on $250 billion in commercial deals, which later never materialized.
The trade war followed in 2018, along with the first stage of the tech war that targeted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei the following year. The Phase One trade deal in early 2020 eased tensions but didn’t stop them from boiling over once more during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Beijing was so concerned by the downturn in relations and the mixed signals out of the White House that it feared an “ October surprise ,” a military strike to rally support before Trump’s presidential race with Democrat Joe Biden.
Gen. Mark Milley, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called his Chinese counterpart without Trump’s knowledge to assure him that the U.S. government was planning no such action—and to preempt any miscalculation by Beijing.
Trump’s last experience as a lame duck president didn’t lead to a hot war, but it locked in a new Cold War with China, one of economic decoupling and export controls. And on the last full day of the first Trump administration, his then secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, accused Xi’s government of genocide against Muslims in far-western China.
On the day Biden took office as the new U.S. president, China sanctioned former senior Trump officials in retaliation for the wild final weeks. The message to the new administration, and indeed the expectation, was that Trump’s hard-line China policies should be walked back. That didn’t happen and the rivalry was institutionalized.
Trump has no reason to hold back if Xi doesn’t play ball. And even with Trump neutered, the Democrats may not play nice.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Cause of death revealed for 22-year-old who died on LA-bound Southwest flight
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Cause of death revealed for 22-year-old who died on LA-bound Southwest flight
articles.content_orig:
The cause of death for a 22-year-old man who died aboard a Southwest flight in August has been revealed.
Rain McMillen Walmsley died from the “combined effects of 7-Hydroxymitragynine and Mitragynine,” according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office. His manner of death is listed as an accident.
7-Hydroxymitragynine and Mitragynine are compounds found in kratom, a plant supplement that has drawn growing concern due to recent overdoses.
Kratom comes from a plant native to Southeast Asia, whose leaves are typically dried and consumed for their stimulant or sedative effects, depending on the dosage. In smaller amounts, the substance can produce effects similar to caffeine.
But 7-Hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, can produce opioid-like effects when its concentration is artificially increased. Kratom is sold widely, but is legal and unregulated. There’s been recent scrutiny about a high risk of abuse of the drug.
Walmsey was aboard Southwest Airlines Flight 958 on August 7. The flight was traveling from Dallas to Los Angeles when Walmsey suffered a medical emergency and stopped responding.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Crew members and fellow passengers attempted to save him, with multiple CPR attempts carried out while the plane continued toward Southern California.
Emergency responders were waiting for the aircraft when it landed at Los Angeles International Airport, but their efforts were unsuccessful.
Paramedics were unable to revive Walmsey, and firefighters pronounced him dead at the scene.
Southwest Airlines previously confirmed that there had been a “medical incident involving a customer” aboard Flight 958 but did not provide additional details about the passenger.
The Irvine City Council, concerned with adverse effects from kratom, recently imposed stricter regulations on the sale and distribution of synthetic kratom. Officials restricted its use to customers 21 and older and established potency limits, banning the sale and distribution of kratom products containing more than 2% 7-OH.
In Mississippi , two college students in separate incidents were found dead with kratom at the scene in September, inflating concern to even higher levels. The Lafayette County Metro Narcotics squad previously said it does “not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Media’s investors lost $2.2 billion while Trump holds $460 million stake
articles.title_zh: Trump Media’s investors lost $2.2 billion while Trump holds $460 million stake
articles.content_orig:
If you’re one of the nearly one million of investors who bought into Donald Trump’s pet crypto coin, the best time to sell was January of 2025, before the whales cashed out and sent prices tumbling. The second best time was yesterday.
Trump’s memecoin has suffered a massive fall-off in the wake of the US midterm elections, tumbling to an all-time-low of $1.12, down from an already paltry $1.70 just prior to the all-important round of voting. Even a month ago, holders of the crypto currency could have gotten out at roughly $2.00 a pop.
Obviously, anybody short-sighted enough to approach Trump coin as an investment is getting pummeled. But with a current market cap of around $340 million, there are clearly more than a few people hoping against hope for a turnaround.
It’s a fitting end for a crypto venture that many had pegged as a grift from the very start. Unfortunately, many more fell for the scam, pumping the coin up to a market cap of $72 billion at its peak.
One analysis found that some 21 well-timed whales pulled the rug on coin holders early into the currency’s launch, getting out with some $214 million and sending the value plummeting.
Predictably, many of the president’s victims count themselves among his biggest fans . In July, the BBC reported that Trump had raked in over $1 billion from all of his crypto dealings combined since returning to the Oval Office in 2025 — money ripped from the hands of the MAGA movement’s most devoted followers.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for ⁠its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal ⁠diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.

Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity
Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law.
The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”.
The residents, who have been unsuccessful in other courts, argue that the evictions by the housing association were intended to cut the number of residents with a “non-western” background in order to stop the area from becoming a “ghetto” and therefore subject to the legislation. The government has previously argued the classification is unrelated to ethnicity.
In December, the European court of justice (ECJ) ruled that the legislation may be unlawful . The law requires housing associations to cut not-for-profit housing by 40%, including by selling or demolishing properties or terminating the lease of tenants by 2030.
It also includes demolishing apartment blocks in areas previously labelled “tough ghettos” (now “transformation areas”) by the government, where at least half of residents have a “non-western” background. Other areas with similar socioeconomic conditions – such as high levels of unemployment or crime – are not subject to these measures.
The policy has been widely criticised by human rights groups including Amnesty International. The European Commission Against Racism and Intolerance published a report last month that said there had been “no positive change in the authorities’ approach to the use of the ‘non-western’ category across various laws, policies and administrative practices, including in relation to the ‘parallel society’ legislation”.
The UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination has called on Danish authorities to stop using the terms “western” and “non-western” in law and policy, and expressed concern that the parallel societies law has a “discriminatory impact on ethnic minorities”.
Residents in Mjølnerparken housing estate in central Copenhagen, who filed a suit against the law in Denmark in 2020 arguing that using their ethnicity to decide where they can live was discriminatory and illegal, have yet to have their case returned to the domestic courts since December’s verdict. More than 1,000 people were forced to move out because of the law.
But legal experts said that the Nøjsomhed-Sydvej case, to be heard on Friday and Monday, could have implications for the Mjølnerparken case because it is likely to lead to a domestic ruling on whether “non-western” background is covered by racial discrimination law.
Susheela Math, the head of legal at the NGO Systemic Justice, said: “If the supreme court decides that ‘non-western’ background is linked to ethnic origin and racial discrimination law, that raises huge questions for the Danish state.”
It would force the Danish state to decide whether it is to abolish the categorisation entirely, which could have ramifications across society, she said.
“[The government] will refer to ethnic origin when it suits them but inside a court, no matter what you present, they say ‘non-western’ background has nothing to do with ethnicity and that they do not collect ethnic data,” said Math.
It is understood that residents of Nøjsomhed-Sydvej would be allowed to return to their homes if they win the case, expected to be decided later this month.
But it is likely to be much more difficult for residents of Mjølnerparken to return to their homes if they win their case when it is heard, because they have been sold.
The Danish ministry of children, senior citizens, and housing has been contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.title_zh: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Friday said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure, even after voters strongly opposed data centers during Tuesday's midterm elections.
"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen in an interview at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital."
Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to the facilities mounted swiftly over the summer as Americans grew worried about their potential to harm the environment, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss.
Investors have turned skeptical on the AI trade of late due to a combination of higher borrowing costs, concerns about soaring debt and public backlash toward the industry. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, led by a plunge in shares of the chipmakers and neocloud companies most closely tied to the AI buildout. The stocks rebounded some on Friday.
OpenAI depends on data centers to train its AI models and serve customers, and Friar said she doesn't think the election results dramatically changed anything for the company. On Thursday, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.
"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said.
OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar said Friday that the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is trying to go public first, with an aim to hit the Nasdaq in mid-November.
Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year jumped roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing.
"The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument."

articles.title_orig: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.title_zh: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The US added 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past economists' expectations, as the labor market showed strength despite the Federal Reserve's recent rate hikes.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% even amid a slight increase in labor force participation. September's underwhelming jobs report of 29,000 additions was also revised upward to a gain of 60,000 jobs.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, deemed the results "a blowout" in a post on X .
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg projected a gain of about 70,000 jobs in October and saw the unemployment rate holding steady. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September, better than expectations for 0.3% month-over-month growth. Annual earnings rose 3.1%, beating expectations but likely still below the current inflation rate.
Employers added jobs in a number of sectors of the economy. Professional and business services, which had been seen as more vulnerable to AI-related disruptions, added 70,000 roles. Healthcare, long a strong spot for job growth, added a higher-than-average 42,000 positions.
Transportation and warehousing jobs rose by 25,000, and manufacturing continued to show strength with 19,000 additions.
"This is still a low-hire, low-fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement.
Other job market measures released earlier this week telegraphed steady hiring — though not to the extent of Friday's report blowout number. Job openings and hiring edged higher , the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed; private employers added 86,000 jobs , according to ADP; and layoff plans dropped to a three-year low while seasonal hiring ramped up.
"Consistent with prior, more partial indicators of the US labor market, the October Jobs Report came in very strong, across the board," Wharton economist Mohamed El-Erian posted on X.
The solid report will likely give the Federal Reserve more confidence to move forward with another rate hike in December . The central bank will also consider November jobs data and October's inflation figures before its Dec. 9 rate decision. Traders currently see a 77% chance of a 25 basis point rate hike next month, up from 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch.
"Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: 20 Years of Gears
articles.title_zh: 20 Years of Gears
articles.content_orig:
It’s hard to believe that 20 years ago, Gears of War launched on XBOX 360 and introduced the world to Marcus Fenix, Dominic Santiago, and the genius of putting a chainsaw on a gun.
Since then, a lot has happened.
We’ve released new games, introduced new characters and enemies, and welcomed millions of players into the world of Gears. But when we think about what makes this franchise special, it’s not just the games or the stories we’ve told. It’s the people who have made Gears of War part of their lives.
Over the years, we’ve heard some incredible stories from our fans. Stories of friendships that started in multiplayer lobbies and have lasted for decades. Of campaign playthroughs with fathers or brothers, or groups of friends who made playing Horde together a weekly tradition. Soldiers that have played during military deployments and couples who met playing Gears, fell in love, and eventually got married. Not bad for a game about chainsawing monsters.
And then there are the stories that hit a little harder. Fans who have shared how Gears helped them through a dark and difficult time, whether it was dealing with loss, feeling isolated, or just needing a few hours with Delta Squad to forget about everything else going on in their lives. Sometimes a familiar game and a few friends on the other end of a headset can make a real difference.
For us at The Coalition, these are the stories that matter most.
We’ve always talked about Gears being a franchise built on brotherhood, loyalty, and having each other’s backs. It’s what makes the relationship between Marcus, Dom and the rest of the Gears so important, and it’s been at the heart of the series since the beginning.
But what’s really special is seeing those same values reflected in the community that’s grown around the games. The friendships, the relationships, the shared experiences, and the sense of belonging that comes from finding your people.
It’s an incredible privilege to steward this franchise, to build on the legacy of the creators at EPIC Games, the voice actors and all the creative collaborators who have had a hand in this universe. And to create games that people care so deeply about.
Thank you for making Gears part of your lives, and for letting us be a small part of yours.
To celebrate our 20 th Anniversary, this week we kicked off a 2-week anniversary event in Gears of War: E-Day featuring limited time modes and new rewards. In Versus, play Guardian, where only one leader makes it out alive. And in Horde Siege, try out the For the Queen mode, where the supply cache is disabled, leaving you and the squad to rely on your loadouts.
Tomorrow is the exact date of our anniversary and to celebrate we’re giving away RAAM as a multiplayer character to every Gears of War: E-Day player as a free gift. Just login to claim him instantly.
And beginning December 1, we launch our next Season – titled Legacy – which continues to honor the greatest hits of Gears over 20 years in our maps, modes and multiplayer skins. Season 2 not only brings back some fan favorites from the history of the franchise but lets us reimagine characters in ways we’ve always wanted to see them – like Solemn Memories Dom, whose character skin depicts him in the suit he’s wearing in the famous photo of him and Maria from Gears of War 2.

articles.title_orig: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign will drop an important button, per leak
articles.title_zh: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign will drop an important button, per leak
articles.content_orig:
Next year Apple is rumored to have a big redesign coming to the iPhone Pro models, and per a new leak, it may come with the loss of the Action button.
2027 brings the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, and all signs indicate Apple has something special planned. Similar to the debut of iPhone X for the 10th anniversary in 2017, Apple may introduce a bold new iPhone design next year.
New iPhone Pro models are rumored to get quad-curved displays that wrap around the edges for a visually bezel-free appearance. Screen size is expected to increase too.
Now today, a new post from leaker Instant Digital on Weibo says this new design will also come with a loss.
Per the post, the Action button will be removed from next year’s iPhone Pro models. The devices will retain a Camera Control button though, similar to iPhone Duo.
Add a gimmick go jack up the price and then drop the gimmick and keep the price. It’s the Touch Bar all over again.
The leaker says the Action button’s functionality won’t be lost altogether, though. Instead, he says Camera Control will continue to launch the Camera app with a standard press, but a long-press will offer Action button-like functionality.
When iPhone Duo dropped the Action button, some users expressed disappointment that the button’s versatility was lost. Our own Chance Miller, for example, said he would gladly give up Camera Control to keep the Action button.
It sounds like Apple plans to integrate the two, a pattern that will likely apply to the next-generation iPhone Duo and other future models too.
What do you think of Apple’s reported plan for the Action button? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_zh: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
articles.content_orig:
Published Nov 6, 2026 at 10:58 a.m. ET
Published Nov 6, 2026 at 10:58 a.m. ET

Google is locked in a standoff with the nation’s largest public school system as the debate over AI’s place in the classroom pits parent groups against the tech behemoth.
Earlier this week, Google said schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose access to Google search, prompting cries of blackmail and a swift rebuke from Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”
In September, Mamdani announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools and tighter limits on screens, especially for the youngest students. The moratorium was a major win for city parents who oppose the use of artificial intelligence in public school classrooms.
But Google’s threat to pull the plug on search in classrooms underscored how deeply the technology’s products are woven into the fabric of education.
Google products are ubiquitous in schools. Since the pandemic, many students have been issued individual Chromebooks for schoolwork and remote learning. City officials said the school system has 1.3 million Chromebooks, with about 500,000 assigned to students, and another 800,000 in schools. Teachers post assignments to Google Classroom, and students, like many adults, rely heavily on Google Docs and search.
“It would be incredibly difficult for us to disentangle our school system entirely from Google, and that's what they're betting on,” said Kelly Clancy, part of the coalition calling for a total ban on AI in the city’s public schools. She said all three of her children are required to use Google Classroom for remote learning and homework.
“But I think what they're not counting on is the fact that parents across the country have mobilized against this,” Clancy said. “And this is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students.”
Google has insisted it’s impossible to separate the company’s search function from AI.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” so turning off AI will also mean turning off the search engine. The company said the new policy would go into effect early next year. It did not respond to Gothamist’s requests for comment.
But over the past year, an influential movement of parents, educators and lawmakers have sought to beat back the creep of artificial intelligence in schools. They argue AI summaries and bots enable cheating, short-circuit learning and seduce children into inappropriate and even dangerous relationships. This week, parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode.
Education officials said they were still trying to figure out how Google’s new policy would affect search in schools.
Officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” public schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said.
She said the city has disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI mode on Google Chromebooks issued to students, and they’ve made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview that continues to appear in search results.
“We will keep students and school communities updated as we continue to place student safety and wellbeing above all other interests,” she said.
Following the Times report, Google posted additional information about its plans on X .
It said the announcements give schools "more choice, not less" and that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will be off by default, and schools will be in charge of which service, if any, is turned on.
The company emphasized the changes were made in response to feedback from K-12 schools. Google said it’s also changing how AI will function within search “to make it better for learning.” The company said both AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guidance through problems” rather than just “quick answers to schoolwork.”
Assemblymember Alex Bores noted that Google has made “deep investments” into its educational offerings over the years, aggressively and successfully marketing its suite of products to schools.
“This is a product choice that Google is making, and it's a profit maximizing one,” said Bores, who worked at Palantir and recently co-founded Who Decides, an advocacy group for AI safety and regulation.
“Competitors like Duck Duck Go let people opt in or opt out of AI search. And Google could do the same. They could also do the same only when it comes to children if they wanted. But they're making an intentional choice not to, and I think that's a disappointing one,” he said.
Anti-AI parents and educators said Google’s threat should encourage the city to cut ties with the company, and invest in other search engines instead. Naveed Hasan, a member of the Panel for Educational Policy, which votes on education contracts, said the city should consider writing limits into contracts to prevent tech companies from unilaterally changing the software the school system has already purchased without permission.
“We should revisit how we look at technology contracts when companies change their features mid contract,” he said.
Zephyr Teachout, professor at Fordham Law School, said the company’s move may also face legal challenges. “What Google is doing is illegal under antitrust law and I expect there will be investigations from the Attorney General’s office and other places soon,” she said. “It’s simply not credible to me that Google cannot provide search without AI overviews.”
Clancy saw an opening for the school system to rethink how it teaches students to do their work.
“This is an exciting opportunity for us to figure out [how] to teach kids the fundamentals of research,” she said.
Maybe instead of spending so much on Google, Clancy added, the city could invest in school libraries and books.
Jessica is the education reporter for WNYC and Gothamist. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jessica reported on the shutdown and reopening of the nation’s largest school system, highlighting the unprecedented impacts on learning, health and mental health for students, staff and families. articles.title_orig: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.title_zh: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.content_orig:
Kenny Polcari discusses the historical S&P 500 performance following midterm elections. He predicts the stock market will be higher in 12 months, continuing a trend seen in every midterm cycle since World War II.
The U.S. economy added jobs at a strong pace in October, rebounding from a softer September amid economic uncertainty.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October. That figure was well above the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by LSEG.
The unemployment rate decreased slightly to 4.1%, which was lower than the expectations of economists who predicted it would hold steady at 4.2%.
Revisions were made to the payroll numbers for the prior two months, with August revised up by 53,000 from a gain of 133,000 jobs to 186,000 jobs; while the change for September was revised up by 31,000 jobs from a gain of 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, employment in August and September was 84,000 higher than previously reported.
TRUMP ADMIN NAMES NEW ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY ZONES TO SPUR PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN STRUGGLING COMMUNITIES
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 jobs in October, well above the 64,000 expected by economists polled by LSEG.
Government payrolls increased by 6,000 jobs in October. The sector's loss of 17,000 jobs in September was revised down to a loss of 18,000 jobs. The federal government shed 1,000 jobs in October, while state governments added 8,000 jobs and local governments cut 1,000 roles last month.
The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs in October, well above the gain of 5,000 that was predicted by economists polled by LSEG. September's gain of 9,000 jobs was also revised up to 13,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, which was well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 jobs over the past 12 months. The sector's job growth was led by gains in professional, scientific and technical services (+32,900), and in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,100).
Healthcare added 41,600 jobs in October, above the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last 12 months. Most of last month's gains were in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+10,500) and outpatient care centers (+4,800).
Transportation and warehousing added 24,800 jobs last month, with growth occurring among couriers and messengers (+17,400) and air transportation (+3,500).
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 in October, well above the expectations of a gain of 64,000 jobs. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
PRIVATE SECTOR ADDED 86,000 JOBS IN OCTOBER, ABOVE EXPECTATIONS, ADP SAYS
The number of long-term unemployed, defined as those who have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, was 2 million in October and changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people.
The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would've preferred full-time work but were working part-time because their hours were reduced, or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
The labor force participation was 61.9% in October, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%. Both of these figures were little changed in October and have shown little net change since January.
Average hourly earnings increased 3.1% year over year in October, above the 2.4% rise predicted by LSEG economists. Earnings also grew 0.4% on a monthly basis, above the 0.3% estimate in the LSEG poll.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and central bank policymakers will hold their next interest rate meeting on December 8-9. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the October jobs report "is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown."
"Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions," Shah said. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that the October jobs report's "payroll number removed the traffic light at the December intersection for the Fed."
"Fed focus was already firmly on moderating inflation , and continued signs of tightening in the labor market give it a license to raise rates without hindering its employment mandate. Additional tightening is possible in the first quarter if inflation continues to print strong," Rosner added.
The strong October jobs report raised the likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates when it holds its next meeting on Dec. 8-9.
The market's expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike ticked up on Friday, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 76.8% probability the Fed hikes in December – an increase from 66.9% a week ago. A hike of that size would take the federal funds rate to a target range of 4% to 4.25%.

The benchmark S&P 500 Index rose 0.65% during Friday morning's trading session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.25%.

articles.title_orig: New PS Plus Perks Revealed, Includes Discounts and Free Trials
articles.title_zh: New PS Plus Perks Revealed, Includes Discounts and Free Trials
articles.content_orig:
Sony has announced a range of new “perks” for PS Plus, including a three-month trial to YouTube Premium, as well as trials and discounts for other services. But not all fans are on board.
"Enjoy a range of special offers, trials and discounts from PlayStation, Sony and select partners. All included with your PlayStation Plus membership," Sony's announcement reads.
Those partners include YouTube Premium, DAZN, Audible, and Sony Pictures' own Core. Elsewhere, PS Plus members get a 5% discount when they buy direct from PlayStation, they can save 10% on gaming and audio from Sony Electronics, and a two month trial of Calm Premium.
"How is a free trial a perk?" one person complained on social media . "Calling free trials a perk is a big reach," another person commented. "These are not real perks, these are just money for Sony by funnelling people into these other subscriptions," another said. "Nobody cares about a free trial. Give us full crunchy roll premium on ps plus and then maybe we will be happy," one person suggested.
Others are using the perks announcement to once again criticize Sony for its decision to kill PlayStation discs from 2028. “Are Physical discs a perk?” said one social media user . “This reeks of desperation,” said another before continuing: “So many people have abandoned PS Plus as a result of Sony’s plans to end physical discs, that they are now trying to entice people with the old carrot and the stick routine.”
The disc backlash does not appear to have affected Sony's bottom line so far. In Sony’s recent financial results , the number of monthly active users (MAUs) across the PlayStation platform actually increased 7% in September compared to the same month of the previous fiscal year to 127 million accounts — that’s a record high for September. Sony said this indicates “the baseline of engagement is steadily improving.”
According to the same results, 78% of game sales over the period were digital, which is a significant majority. With digital sales of first-party games, Sony gets the full cut of revenue.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay’s Peña loses top aides as impeachment trial resumes over failed bank
articles.title_zh: Paraguay’s Peña loses top aides as impeachment trial resumes over failed bank
articles.content_orig:
Why is Paraguay facing a banking and political crisis?
Lawmakers in Paraguay have resumed impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Pena, a day after he resigned amid links to the country’s worst financial crisis in decades.
The Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove the conservative economist from office.
Politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president on Thursday, despite his resignation. Pena, who was elected in 2023, has requested a 72-hour extension to prepare his defence before the Senate.
The proceedings follow a vote in Paraguay’s lower house of Congress, where lawmakers overwhelmingly approved impeachment charges against Pena in a 78-0 vote.
The political turmoil surrounding the country’s president follows Paraguay’s central bank’s intervention earlier this week at Ueno Bank, one of the country’s fastest-growing digital lenders, citing breaches of minimum solvency requirements.
Pena previously held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, until last year, when he claims he sold his shares. Paraguayan lawmakers have accused the president of a conflict of interest and questioned whether authorities failed to act on warnings about the lender’s financial position.
The collapse of Ueno, which held $850m in public funds, has left more than half of Paraguay’s population without access to their accounts, drawing intense scrutiny over the government’s relationship with the bank and financial regulators’ effectiveness.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds — as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans — be protected,” Pena said in a Thursday video address where he apologised for failing to prevent the crisis.
The crisis has also prompted the resignation of Paraguay’s central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, and arrest warrants for eight Ueno executives, who later turned themselves in.
Paraguay’s attorney general has ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, including its regulatory oversight and the placement of public funds in the institution.
If Pena is convicted in an impeachment trial, he would lose the lifetime Senate seat and associated legal protections ordinarily granted to former Paraguayan presidents.

articles.title_orig: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.title_zh: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.content_orig:
David Blair was a foreign correspondent for nearly 20 years, reporting from 60 countries across Africa, Asia and the Middle East. He then joined the Foreign Office and later No 10, where he wrote speeches and advised three Foreign Secretaries and one Prime Minister. He returned to The Telegraph as Chief Foreign Affairs Commentator in 2025.
When Jared Kushner declares that any Ukraine peace settlement must include the “broader European security architecture”, we do not have to guess what the US envoy means.
Vladimir Putin spelt it out for us almost five years ago.
That phrase is diplomatic code for Putin’s demand, made public in December 2021, for the entire system of European security to be overturned to cripple Nato and restore Russia’s overlordship of its old empire.
Back then, Russia’s leader released a full draft treaty with nine articles, Article 4 of which would have banned Nato from deploying “military forces and weaponry” in any of the 16 countries that joined the alliance after May 27, 1997.
The consequence would have been that every ally east of Germany, including Poland, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states, would have seen their Nato membership rendered meaningless at a stroke. After all, if allies cannot send troops to defend one another’s territory, they are no longer allies in any real sense.
That particular demand from Putin came with the sort of fake concession for which Russian diplomacy is famed. Yes, military deployments could be allowed in Nato’s post-1997 members in “exceptional cases”, perhaps if such a country had to “eliminate a threat to security”, but only “with the consent of all the parties”, which would include Russia.
So Nato could only send forces to repel a Russian invasion of Latvia, for example, if Russia would first agree to its own invasion being repelled. If, by some extraordinary chance, the invader did not agree, then Nato would have to abandon Latvia to Russia’s mercy.
That is what Putin means – and has always meant – when he talks of a new European security architecture. He means a system that clears Nato out of the way and leaves him free to invade any neighbour.
Every previous US administration understood that perfectly well, which is why Europe and the then president, Joe Biden, united to reject Russia’s proposal in December 2021, whereupon Putin showed exactly why he wanted the ability to attack his neighbours by launching an onslaught against Ukraine two months later.
President Trump today advanced an important discussion with several European leaders about the need for a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace.

Building on his leadership and the substantive work undertaken this week in Brussels with Ukraine, NATO, and our European partners, @SEPeaceMissions and I wanted to share some of the objectives guiding our ongoing discussions.

For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework. Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.

Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.

We are exploring five principal goals: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.

Any arrangements must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of every nation. Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another's sovereign choices. NATO will remain central to European collective defense, and this initiative would build upon existing institutions and commitments.

We will continue consultations through the Shell Bay format with Ukraine, NATO, the EU, and our European partners, expanding engagement to ensure that all relevant perspectives and ideas are considered. We will also engage Russia as part of the peace negotiations.

Next week in Abu Dhabi, the United States will convene the first trilateral peace discussions with Ukraine and Russia since February. All parties remain intensely engaged in preparing for substantive and productive negotiations. We will consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines and, if progress is made, aim to move toward a broader multilateral format with their direct participation.

These ideas continue to evolve, and we welcome thoughtful input. Creating the right structure will be critical to ending this war and transitioning from conflict toward conditions that make possible a durable peace.

This is difficult, detailed work. There are no easy solutions. But the opportunity to help end this devastating war and build a foundation for a more peaceful, secure, and prosperous Europe for generations to come makes it a challenge well worth undertaking.

We will see how these discussions develop and continue working intensively with all parties toward President Trump's objective of a comprehensive and lasting peace.
But today things are not so simple. Who would trust Donald Trump to oppose Putin’s vision of reducing central Europe to a helpless playground for Russian aggression?
The American president is already looking ahead to the trilateral peace talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week and talking about how a “big agreement” is coming “and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine”.
Fortunately, accepting Putin’s plan and granting Russia the freedom to rebuild its empire by trampling European countries one by one is not entirely within Mr Trump’s gift.
Even if the US president were to suddenly agree to withdraw all American troops from Nato’s post-1997 members, that would still leave 1,000 British soldiers in Estonia, alongside 2,000 Canadians in Latvia, 2,000 Germans in Lithuania, and thousands more deployed by other allies in nearby states.
The US Congress has also carefully bound Mr Trump’s hands by passing the National Defence Authorisation Act of 2025, which specifies that a minimum of 76,000 US military personnel must stay in Europe.
So Mr Trump cannot give Putin what he most wants – a total US military withdrawal from Europe – nor can he compel other Nato members to abandon their allies by bringing their soldiers home.
In the same statement, Mr Kushner offered reassurance that any new European security arrangements would not allow any country to have a “veto over another’s sovereign choices”, which seems incompatible with Russia being able to block deployments in Nato’s post-1997 members.
So we know what Putin wants because it was published almost five years ago. We know that Trump alone cannot give him what he wants. We also know that the spectre of a grand bargain between the two leaders has been revived.
But the reality is that no bilateral settlement agreed by Russia and America above Europe’s head could work, regardless of how much the two mutually-regarding titans in the Kremlin and the White House may wish otherwise.
Europe has the collective ability to block any new security system. It should not sell that bargaining power for cheap.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

articles.title_orig: Why Micron’s Stock Valuation Now Looks Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: Why Micron’s Stock Valuation Now Looks Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Over the past few months, Micron ( MU ), the leading AI chip memory maker, has seen shares plunge due to a mix of cyclicality and pricing fears, political policy concerns, and profit taking. Let's unpack why these fears are overblown:
Micron bears argue that the record-high DRAM and NAND pricing may have a reached a peak and increased competition will only exacerbate these concerns. However, there is no evidence to support this bearish argument. Micron has confirmed that 2026 and 2027 capacity is completely sold out. Additionally, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrota believes that tight memory storage supply conditions will persist through 2028.
Wall Street analysts agree with this bull scenario. Zacks Consensus Analyst Estimates suggest that Micron's earnings and sales will maintain explosive, triple-digit year-over-year earnings and sales growth through 2027.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
The Democratic sweep of in the midterm elections has raised investor concerns of legislative scrutiny that will slow down the massive AI data center buildout. However, the market and AI stocks have been pricing in a Democratic sweep for months. Additionally, hyperscaler CAPEX spending is expected to explode to $1.4 trillion next year. In other words, regardless of who is in office, there is no evidence that the AI buildout is slowing.
Image Source: Carson Investment Research
Because of its rare mix of liquidity, triple-digit top-and-bottom line growth, and stock performance, Micron has attracted numerous institutional investors like David Tepper over the past few years. After a 1,000% upside move, some profit taking is to be expected. However, Micron shares are retreating to the 200-day moving average for the first time. The 200-day moving average provides an attractive reward-to-risk zone for investors because institutional investors tend to "defend" leaders at this level. Additionally, the 200-day moving average provides investors with a logical risk level to trade against.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
Over the past decade, Micron's average historical price-to-earnings ratio has been ~20x. Today, its valuation is currently 11x. For context, the S&P 500's current P/E ratio is ~18x. Meanwhile, Micron's forward P/E ratio is an unheard of ~5x.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
As AI evolves from simple text generation to agents and robots, Micron will experience even more demand. For example, robots and robotaxis rely on the continuous sensory data that Micron provides. In addition, agentic AI platforms performing multi-step work flows require immense memory.
Despite recent market jitters over pricing cyclicality, political policies, and profit-taking, the underlying fundamentals for Micron remain exceptionally strong. With memory capacity fully booked through 2027, robust hyperscaler spending, an attractive valuation near key technical support, and long-term tailwinds from agentic and physical AI, this pullback offers an appealing entry point for long-term investors.

Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that eight ships have been attacked so far this week in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since July 6, a total of 63 of 88 projectile strikes happened along a southern route near the coastline of Oman, according to the UKMTO.
There were also three ships attacked this week in the Arabian Gulf, it added.
"Of the 11 incidents, 3 continued their voyage, 5 required assistance and 3 Vessels sunk," the UKMTO said in a weekly overview, noting that the risk for ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz remains "severe."
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., accused Pete Hegseth of "wasting taxpayer dollars" after the secretary of war posted a video to social media Thursday defending the Iran war and calling on Congress to approve a $350 billion budget request.
"Pete Hegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way," Tillis said in a post on X Friday.
"This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to the president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters," he added.
Tillis previously has called on President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth.
Ali Akbar Velayati, an advisor to Iran's supreme leader on international affairs, said Friday that, "Any energy or transit corridor that tries to bypass us will either become too expensive or unstable."
"Now that everyone is talking about the new order of West Asia, it should be noted that: Iran is a bridge between [the] Persian Gulf, Central Asia, Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added on X.
"The domino effect of crises from Gaza to the Red Sea, and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone experiences collective insecurity."
“The tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia has engulfed the elections in Israel and the United States. The result: ‘Iran is now one of the principal architects of the regional order — a reality that can neither be eliminated nor replaced’,” Velayati also was quoted as saying Friday by Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to reports, as disagreements over the conflict expose tensions within the Trump administration and raise questions about Vance's potential 2028 presidential ambitions.
The clash, reported by Axios Nov. 4., comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections and Vance publicly blamed the war for the party's defeat while urging President Donald Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than renewed military strikes.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote later on Wednesday on X.
"Low-level hostility between Vance and Netanyahu is beneficial for Vance," Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital.
"It allows him to give some distance from the Trump administration, which has just taken a huge electoral beating, but also to position himself ... in a very different position than President Trump himself without attacking Trump."
Qatar said Friday that President Donald Trump called its leader Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani to discuss "the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that a tanker ship traveling through the Strait of Hormuz reported an explosion.

Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Col. Turki al-Malki said Friday that the country's air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles "launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Najran."
