articles.title_orig: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.content_orig:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.content_orig:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.
Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.
Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.
South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.
Christopher Forbes , head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets , called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining ( via Reuters ):
double quotation mark “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out.
“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.
“And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”
After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.
Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.
Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA , down over 9%.
Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector .
Kyle Rodda , senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.
double quotation mark The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom.
The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.
So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.
7am GMT: Lloyds house price index
9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index
1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report
3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report
Interestingly, Jefferies economist Mohit Kumar doesn’t believe yesterday’s losses are “the start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
double quotation mark We do admit that policy uncertainty after the Blue Tsunami raises concerns over AI investment and the pace of data center buildup.
However, data centers and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move onto other states or outside the country. AI investment has been a key driver of US growth, and we do not see Democrats as giving up on this growth engine.
There was a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the US stock market yesterday, Jim Reid of Deutche Bank told clients this morning:
double quotation mark In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020 . And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025 .
So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March.
Mohit Kumar, economist at investent bank Jefferies , doesn’t expect a quick rebound from yesterday’s losses.
double quotation mark In previous episodes of retail selling, institutional investors have stepped in to find value. The approaching year-end complicates the behaviour of institutional accounts as risk appetite would be limited….
The geopolitical uncertainty around possible US action in Iran also suggests that investors would not rush to add risk.
Stuart Clark , portfolio manager at Quilter , points out that the dominance of the tech sector exacerbated yesterday’s selloff:
double quotation mark “The blue wave at the ballot box has quickly been replaced by a sea of red on investors’ screens. Technology stocks have sold off sharply, with the immediate catalyst appearing to be concerns around tougher AI regulation, covering both the models themselves and the vast data centre infrastructure required to support them.
“The scale of the falls in some of the market’s biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in US equity markets. With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500.
Ahead of this week’s losses, there were plenty of warning signs that markets might have risen too fast.
As my colleague Richard Partington and I wrote in late September, the warning lights were “flashing red” as the fighting in the Middle East intensified, a slowdown loomed in the AI arms race, and government borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – had risen to its highest level since 2000 by September, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
This week’s losses have pulled the CAPE ratio down ( you can see it here ), but it’s still historically high:
Amid the scary-everything-is-bad-in-stocks news, it’s easy to feel a bit worried about pensions or savings, my colleague Siraj Datoo writes.
And yes, yesterday was a bad day in particular for technology stocks, with the Nasdaq losing $2.5tn in market capital in a single day.
But it’s worth taking a second to pause. While many of the charts leading newspaper homepages are fairly narrow, showing the dramatic fall in just a few days, if you look at the Nasdaq, the US index mostly dominated by tech stocks, from the start of the year, it’s still up 4.6% YTD ( see previous post for more details ).
Of course, this correction still could have room to run and markets are famously emotional. But there have been warnings about this. Michael Burry, the famous fund manager behind The Big Short, has been screaming from the sidelines about overvaluations in the tech world.
One of the major concerns right now is the huge data centre buildout in the US and whether Democrats will place restrictions or slow things down. That’s a problem for investors because so many of the world’s biggest companies have invested enormous amounts of money -- often taking on additional debt -- to fund their deep investment. The bet is that the artificial buildout will eventually generate big returns but investors are now increasingly worried about just how long that will take.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s Congress has refused to accept President Santiago Pena’s resignation, pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings after the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank.
President since 2023, Pena had attempted to resign on Thursday as millions of Ueno customers remained unable to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” the conservative politician said in a recorded address.
But lawmakers declined to accept his resignation. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings, summoning him to appear on Friday.
A joint congressional session called to consider the resignation lost its quorum after lawmakers from Pena’s Colorado Party walked out, as it became clear there were not enough votes to accept it.
Horacio Cartes, a leader in the Colorado Party, had posted a statement on social media indicating the group supported Pena’s impeachment.
“We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds,” Cartes, a former president, wrote in his statement. “We must think of the people and the values we uphold in the Colorado Party.”
Denying Pena’s resignation is likely to heighten the legal jeopardy he faces.
Ordinarily, in Paraguay, presidents who leave office become senators for life, and they enjoy a degree of legal immunity from prosecution as members of the legislature.
But that status is not conferred if the president is convicted in an impeachment trial.
The political crisis erupted earlier this week, when Paraguay’s central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal solvency ratio. Once its books were corrected, the bank’s capital – the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses – was less than half the legal minimum.
Before its collapse, the company claimed it had about 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people. Many have since lost access to their accounts and to pensions paid out through the bank.
As part of a resolution to address the bank’s collapse, Paraguay’s central bank voted to transfer its remaining funds to other financial institutions.
But the central bank itself came under scrutiny for not properly regulating Ueno. The central bank’s head, Carlos Carvallo, has since resigned.
Pena himself formerly held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, though he said he sold those shares in 2025.
Lawmakers, however, have accused Pena of having a conflict of interest and have questioned whether there was an institutional cover-up linked to the lender’s collapse.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“As I speak, there are people outside urging Congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Until its demise, Ueno had grown quickly from a niche company into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850m in public funds.
Paraguay’s attorney general has also ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, which will look into oversight of the lender and the placement of public funds in the institution. Pena has said he will cooperate with investigators.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
If Pena is ultimately removed from office, Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over as president.
Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

articles.title_orig: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.title_zh: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.title_zh: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

articles.title_orig: The Nasdaq Plunges 5%. What the Data Center Crash Means for Investors
articles.title_zh: The Nasdaq Plunges 5%. What the Data Center Crash Means for Investors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Is the AI bubble bursting?
That question was on the minds of millions of investors on Thursday, as the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) had one of its worst days ever, plunging 5.5% as fears spread that a political backlash could choke the AI boom, following the midterm election.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Investors believe that election winners in Texas and elsewhere will slap significant restrictions or even outright bans on data centers, which became a lightning rod during the campaign. After chip stocks were among the few losers on Wednesday, they collapsed on Thursday, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF losing 11.2%. Even industry leader Nvidia lost 9.1%, and the crash triggered a broader sell-off across the stock market, with all 11 sectors falling, even defensive ones like utilities and consumer staples.
Image source: Getty Images.
AI infrastructure stocks began to wobble a few weeks ago, starting with a chart showing that neocloud operator CoreWeave's (NASDAQ:CRWV) bond yields had risen as high as 15%, and worries about a potential default sent the stock tumbling.
Earnings reports from the big hyperscalers were greeted similarly, as investors worried about soaring capital expenditures and negative free cash flow, even as these companies continue to grow rapidly and are hugely profitable.
Then, the election happened, and now fears of a slowdown in the data center build-out have led investors to flee AI stocks .
Stock market reactions to elections are famously rash and often fleeting. Stocks tumbled following the Brexit decision before bouncing back over the following days, and stocks plunged overnight when President Trump was first elected before turning green the following day.
This looks like a similar reaction. Tech stocks initially fell on Tuesday night before the Nasdaq jumped on Wednesday. The response is understandable as data centers have been a major talking point during the campaign, but the sell-off seems like an overreaction.
Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, campaigned on a temporary moratorium on data centers and reasonable guidelines, like a ban on subsidies for data centers. However, she is no radical, telling CNN, "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."
In a worst-case scenario with a significant slowdown in data center construction in the U.S., most industry observers believe that activity would just move abroad, meaning that industry growth wouldn't be significantly impacted.
In an interview with the Motley Fool, Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) CFO Jason Child explained his thinking on the matter, saying, "Let's just say it (the data centers) all slows down. Do we believe AI demand will slow down? I think, generally, most people say no. The genie is out of the bottle." Child also said he was generally skeptical of any political reaction and said the bipartisan interest in economic growth was too strong for there to be a significant slowdown in the build-out. He also noted that Arm could still benefit from a slowdown in data center construction, as Arm's chips excel at performance per watt, which would be in greater demand if data center construction were artificially limited.
Predicting where the data center debate goes from here isn't easy, but Child is right that demand for AI is strong and is unlikely to be shaken by any slowdown in capacity growth.
Meanwhile, many of the top AI stocks are looking cheaper than ever. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) now trades at a forward P/E of less than 20, and it's nearly doubling its revenue each quarter. Micron (NASDAQ:MU), the memory chip leader, is trading at a forward P/E of less than 4.
Many of these AI stocks have already soared this year, so the pullback needs to be seen in that context, but like "Liberation Day" and other political issues that have rocked markets, this response seems likely to be an overreaction and a non-issue within the next year. Buying the dip on quality stocks like Nvidia looks like a smart move.

articles.content_orig:
The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC's Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic.
Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron tumbled 17%, GE Vernova dropped 7% and Sandisk plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday's session.
"I wish I could say that today's flush was the bottom," the " Mad Money " host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn't believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today's AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.
"But I look at the charts, and there still seems like there's no support for so many Tech stocks, especially the semis, because they ran so much on the way up. However it might feel, it's actually an orderly decline because unlike 2000, these are mostly lucrative companies with stocks that went too high."
Investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely, Cramer said. Smaller developers such as CoreWeave , Iren and Nebius face particular risks because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays.
"That's what I am chiefly worried about," he said. "That's the real problem. That's what could really hurt the stock market. ... Right now, no one of significance is defaulting on their debt. The only issue with the debt is that it's connected to those neocloud companies that I mentioned. That's not enough to sink us."
Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could help the market work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged downturn.
"I for one am glad they are ripping the Band-Aid off this market rather than slowing trying to take it off a little bit each day," he said.
For investors, Cramer recommended maintaining sufficient cash. While semiconductor stocks could face further declines, he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and the possibility of an end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism.
"If you have cash you won't panic," Cramer concluded. "You won't be complacent, either. You will be clear-headed and that's how you will lose less money until things get better. They always do."

As Democrats continue to add to their “blue tsunami” of midterms wins, President Donald Trump has pointed the finger of blame at the opposition and at the American public for Thursday’s stock market plunge.
The Nasdaq Composite dipped 5.52 percent while the S&P 500 dropped 4.36 percent and the Dow Jones went down 1,833.06 points in response to this week’s resounding election results.
“The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats.”
In a follow-up post, he told the electorate: “You only have yourselves to blame!”
With votes still being counted in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and elsewhere, Democrats currently hold a 54 to 44 majority in the Senate and are projected to win 253 seats in the House to the GOP’s 157.
The results come amid a civil war brewing within the Trump administration, with insiders scrambling to assign blame, the president reportedly sounding out advisors on the potential firing of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly on “resignation watch.”
The new Democratic senator for Michigan has been busy doing the media rounds since his triumph on Tuesday and yesterday laid out his top three priorities for his party in Congress, also issuing a timely warning against complacency.
El-Sayed remains a hot topic on Fox News, where Laura Ingraham appeared to agree with him about the war and former deputy FBI director Dan Bongino attacked him with an astonishing lack of self-awareness.
A federal judge has temporarily blocked Trump’s administration from constructing a 250-foot “triumphal” arch that the president wants to use as a “top-grade military complex” to tower over Washington, D.C.
The late Thursday decision from District Judge Tanya Chutkan arrived within an hour of a federal planning commission filled with Trump’s allies approving the plans, following several hours of public comments urging the panel to reject it.
Alex Woodward has the latest.
Speaking in the Oval Office Thursday – where he was, again, largely preoccupied with the decor – the president confirmed holding talks with Vladimir Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, or, as he described him “head person of Russia” at the White House but admitted he did not meet with visiting Ukrainian officials.
“I can’t tell you what I discussed,” Trump said of his meeting with Dmitriev but did trail a “big agreement” forthcoming.
The president may be working hard to avoid taking responsibility for Tuesday’s disaster but here’s the great Kaitlan Collins with a timely reminder of his culpability.
As we’ve just seen, the president was last heard from blaming the Democrats for Thursday’s stock dip.
Now, it’s your fault for voting them in – at least according to his latest Truth Social post.
“The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday – So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!”
President Donald Trump has blamed Thursday’s stock market nose-dive on Democrats’ midterm victories – an assessment with which few would argue.
“The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!” Trump wrote on Truth Social after the closing bell rang Thursday.
“It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped.
“Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!”
While Trump’s online rants typically are exaggerated or sprinkled with falsehoods, it is accurate to say that the blue tsunami in reliably Republican states Tuesday also hit Wall Street.
Democrats inflicted a string of historic defeats in the midterm elections against Republicans, allowing them to take control of both chambers of Congress.
The fate of Donald Trump’s final years in the White House will be significantly influenced by the midterm results, as his political opponents gain essential power over policymaking. With control of both chambers, Democrats can now serve as a check on Trump’s most extreme policies.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election, along with 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.
With the majority of preliminary results declared, Democrats are expected to hold at least 54 seats in the Senate after a series of victories in former Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, Maine and Iowa.
After the blue tsunami, Donald Trump has shown off a new red hat.
The president displayed the cap that read “VETO” in the Oval Office Thursday, alluding to his power to reject legislation that he doesn’t like from Democrats once they take control of Congress.
Ruby red Texas went so blue during the GOP’s crushing midterm defeat that Democrat James Talarico got more early votes than Republican Ken Paxton got in total.
Talarico defeated Paxton with more than 5.4 million votes in a blue tsunami that hit their state and other reliably Republican states such as Iowa and Kansas.
Paxton got 4,249,373 total votes, including 3,232,667 early votes, according to data from Texas Secretary of State Robert S. Howden’s office, last updated late Thursday afternoon.
Talarico got nearly 150,000 more votes from Texans who cast their ballots before Election Day than Paxton’s total vote tally. The Democrat got a total of 5,444,982 votes, including 4,397,474 early votes.

articles.title_orig: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears
articles.title_zh: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears
articles.content_orig:
Trillions of dollars have been wiped off the stock value of major tech firms in the US, Europe and Asia after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) development.
In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index fell 5.5% on Thursday, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses.
Investors appear worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates   expressed their opposition to the data centres that are needed to power the technology.
The share falls comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
The sell-off in US stocks on Thursday meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9% and other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Tech stocks in Europe were also hit, with shares in chipmaker Infineon down by more than 8.5% while tech equipment manufacturer ASML dropped 6.5%.
The sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.
In South Korea, chipmaker SK Hynix fell more than 10% and Samsung was down 6.4%. The Kospi share index ended the day down 6%.
The falls mark a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Later on Thursday night he appeared to take aim at voters too.
"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social.
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off in US stocks had sent shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction.
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have also become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .

articles.title_orig: Stocks plunge as election outcome and AI worries crush tech shares
articles.title_zh: Stocks plunge as election outcome and AI worries crush tech shares
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Trump’s D.C.-area arch approved by federal planning commission as court battle looms
Stocks plummeted Thursday, as a blue wave of victories by anti-AI candidates from Maine to Alaska added to already growing fears about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value, as investors stepped back to evaluate new risks to the billions of dollars in investments that have poured into the AI sector.
The S&P 500 plunged 4.4%, erasing $2.8 trillion from the index’s value. Both indexes suffered their worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, fell more than 5.5% and tumbled into “correction” territory, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Markets had largely expected Democrats to win majorities in Congress. But they did not anticipate the scale of the victories, or the upset wins of candidates like Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, the largest data center market in the country.
Democrats still hope to clinch Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska. But already, hundreds of candidates who pledged to rein in AI data centers have been elected to office, raising the prospect of increased regulation on an industry that is the primary driver of U.S. economic growth.
Trump weighed in Thursday to blame the plummeting of stocks on Democrats.
“The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social . “It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE.”
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq Composite is still up by more than 30%, despite recent fears that have sharply driven down chip, memory, and other AI- and cloud computing-linked stocks.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
The selling continued as Asian markets opened on Friday morning local time. Korea’s Kospi index plunged 8%, triggering a market-wide trading halt. AI data center suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix fell by at least 9% in early trading.  Japan’s Nikkei 225 index tumbled 3%.
The commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections hit investors hard Thursday, after stocks initially rallied, on what many said was relief that the results of the midterms were projected quickly and clearly.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
Democrats who won other state and federal offices have also voiced concerns about the industry and its companies.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
On paper, both of Musk’s companies have shed more than $400 billion in value since Tuesday’s election results.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
Arm Holdings slid 13%, while Qualcomm tumbled 9.5%.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index sold off by 12.3%, its worst day since March 2020, when the coronavirus pandemic began to shutter the economy. The “DRAM” ETF, which tracks firms that manufacture computer memory, sank almost 18%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
SanDisk shares plummeted 22%, Micron, Western Digital and AMD fell 17%, while Seagate fell 16%. All of those firms were among the worst performing S&P 500 stocks.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. Brent crude oil ended the day up by 3.8%. U.S. crude oil rose 2.7% on Thursday.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
In the wake of the market moves, traders dialed back bets that the Federal Reserve would raise rates during its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Odds are currently around 60%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833 points or 3.4%. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 9.2%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 6%.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Allie Canal is a business reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Trump Threatens To 'Destroy' Iran, Tehran Sends Nuke Proposal With 7 Terms
articles.title_zh: Trump Threatens To 'Destroy' Iran, Tehran Sends Nuke Proposal With 7 Terms
articles.content_orig:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process “.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack .
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

NVDA fell 15% from its October 6 high as 47 AI and chip stocks shed roughly $5 trillion in market value over three weeks.
Hedge funds have cut stock exposure by more than 8% since June, marking their biggest retreat since 2017, and they are now underweight AI for the first time since early 2023.
Goldman Sachs said the sell-off looks closer to its start than its end, with hedge funds' AI holdings still ranking in the top 17% historically.

NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) closed November 2 at $202.06. That was down 1.26% for the day and 15.54% below its October 6 close of $239.24, which was its highest close of the past year. Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) fell 1.36% to $681.09, which leaves it 10.34% under its October 6 high of $759.66.
Yahoo Finance counted 47 AI and chip stocks that have lost about $5 trillion in market value since October 6. The biggest losers in Yahoo Finance's count were NVIDIA ($835 billion), Alphabet ( NASDAQ:GOOGL ) ($835 billion), SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ) ($505 billion) and TSMC ( NYSE:TSM ) ($395 billion), while the 625 other large U.S. stocks in the same count added about $1.3 trillion.
Morgan Stanley runs a prime brokerage desk, which finances and clears trades for hedge funds. Morgan Stanley's data reportedly show funds underweight the broader AI trade for the first time since early 2023, after they cut total stock exposure by more than 8% since June, the biggest retreat since at least 2017, and much of that positioning shift is likely still ahead.

24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now . Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.

Goldman Sachs data show hedge funds sold AI stocks for five straight days in October, reversing every AI purchase made since the start of 2025. On the biggest day, per Goldman Sachs, they sold shares they owned about 3.5 times faster than they opened new short positions.
A short position profits when a stock falls. Selling existing holdings at that pace looks like de-risking to protect gains more than a bearish call on AI demand.
Underweight means funds hold less of the broad AI trade than their benchmarks do. That usually helps a sell-off end, because fewer holders are left to sell.
Goldman Sachs also said the unwind looks closer to its start than its end. Goldman Sachs data show funds' AI holdings still rank in the top 17% of the past three years, and the Magnificent Seven were net sold in four of the last five trading sessions. A Nomura note put hedge funds' sensitivity to those seven stocks at the 97th percentile as of October 26.
NVIDIA was QQQ's largest holding in the fund's June 30 portfolio filing. That is why the fund fell less than NVIDIA but still fell sharply.
Because the rest of the market rose, money moved around within stocks. After hours on November 2, NVIDIA traded at $203.80 and QQQ at $682.58, slightly above their closes.
Federal Reserve data going back to 1945 show stocks made up a record 48% of household and nonprofit financial assets in the second quarter, up from 39% at the dot-com peak. The richest 10% of households own 88% of stocks.
Those households do much of the country's spending. That is why Bank of America economists called a sustained correction in the AI trade "one of the larger risks to the US and global economy."
NVIDIA's fundamentals look stronger than its recent price action. Second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion beat the $92.07 billion consensus, and the company guided third-quarter revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%.
NVIDIA is still worth $4.88 trillion, but at roughly 13 times forward earnings, the stock already prices in much of the positioning risk. Crowding in the mega caps is still high, so a weak report on November 17, a date NVIDIA has not yet confirmed, could set off another round of selling.
Even a beat may not end the selling, because if NVIDIA beats estimates and still trades below its November 2 close of $202.06, bearish sentiment and broader market forces can drive the stock lower before a recovery.

articles.title_orig: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.title_zh: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.content_orig:
By ZHAO JIA | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-06 10:09
China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening friendly ties and sharing experience in party governance, marking the latest in a series of high-level exchanges between the two neighbors.
The commitments were made on Thursday when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in Beijing with a Workers' Party of Korea delegation led by Kim Song-nam, a member of the Political Bureau, secretary and international department director of the Central Committee of the WPK.
Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, said China stands ready to work with the DPRK to implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and countries, deepen bilateral relations and deliver greater benefits to both peoples.
Close exchanges between President Xi Jinping, who is also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, and Kim Jong-un, general secretary of the WPK and president of the State Affairs of the DPRK, have guided the continued improvement of bilateral ties, Wang said.
In particular, he said Xi's state visit to the DPRK in June saw the two leaders reach a series of important common understandings, charting the course for bilateral relations in the new era.
Briefing the delegation on the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, Wang said the most important outcome was the adoption of the resolution on certain major issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
The resolution carries major immediate significance and provides long-term guidance for strengthening the Party and advancing the building of a strong country and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, he said.
China stands ready to strengthen exchanges of experience and mutual learning with the DPRK on party and state governance to support the development of both parties and advance the socialist cause in both countries, he added.
Kim Song-nam said the deep friendship and strategic guidance of the two leaders form the fundamental cornerstone of China-DPRK friendship, while socialism is their shared ideal, banner and cause.
Pyongyang is willing to work with Beijing to make tireless efforts to advance China-DPRK friendly relations, he added.
Thursday's meeting came within two weeks after Kim Jong-un paid a visit to Dandong, Liaoning province.
Exchanges and cooperation between the two countries have deepened across various fields over the past two years. Bilateral trade in the first half of this year reached its highest level for the period since 2018.
International passenger train services, Air China flights and operations at land border crossings have all fully resumed this year. The New Yalu River Bridge, opened on Oct 15, is expected to further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges.
Yang Danzhi, a research fellow at the National Institute of International Strategy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said deepening practical cooperation and exchanges on state governance and party building helps carry forward the revolutionary legacy and traditional friendship between the two parties and countries and opens a new chapter in China-DPRK relations.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Traders Wrong-Footed After Bullish Equity Calls
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Traders Wrong-Footed After Bullish Equity Calls
articles.content_orig:
A sudden wave of selling swept through U.S. equities on Thursday as hedge funds kept dumping tech XLK positions and anxiety over physical infrastructure constraints sparked a broad retreat across the semiconductors SMH .
The meltdown was broad across the major indexes, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite COMP bearing the brunt of the retreat, plunging 5.4%. The S&P 500 ( SP500 ) dropped 4.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJI declined 3.2%.
Just a day after logging one of its busiest trading days of the year—when markets rallied on the outcome of the midterm elections, which delivered a major victory for Democrats in both the Senate and the House of Representatives—Goldman Sachs’ equities desk observed a market suddenly devoid of buyers and dominated by top-down macro selling.
Long-only institutional investors remained frozen on the sidelines following heavy de-risking into midterms, while hedge funds actively offloaded hyperscaler MSFT AMZN GOOG GOOGL META holdings purchased just a day prior, Goldman partner John Flood wrote in an intraday note.
The wide selloff drove heavy volume spikes relative to 20-day averages—up 160% in the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY , 150% in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF SMH , 100% in the Invesco QQQ Trust QQQ , and 75% in DRAM DRAM -related products—compounded by a second straight day of heavy retail selling skews, the note said. articles.title_orig: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.
The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.
In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.
Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.
In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 9.6%. Electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry , also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology fell 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively, as the regional technology rout deepened.
China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%.
The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday. He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.
"If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."

articles.title_orig: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.title_zh: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.content_orig:
Navy and Marine Corps leaders have recently come to the agreement that the Corps needs 40 amphibious ships to meet its goal of keeping three Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) deployed at the same time. However, at the moment, the Navy has only 31 of these vessels, a minimum mandated by Congress, and now an effort is underway to convince lawmakers to increase the fleet.
MEUs, made up of about 2,200 Marines, are typically embarked on Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), which usually consist of an assault ship, two transport docks or dock landing ships. Support vessels, surface combatants and in some cases a nuclear fast attack submarine can make up the larger Expeditionary Strike Group.
Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Eric Smith’s top priority is meeting what is called the 3.0 ARG/MEU presence, said Shon Brodie, director of Maritime Expeditionary Warfare at the Corps’ Combat Development and Integration (CD&I) Directorate tasked with modernizing the Marines.
Smith “believes that the best thing that we as a service can do for the nation is provide the highly trained Marine Expeditionary Units, one from the East Coast, one from the West Coast, and that one in Japan, persistently,” Brodie told a small group of reporters, including from TWZ , on Wednesday.
To ensure that happens, Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO) Adm. James W. Kilby and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps (ACMC) Gen. Bradford J. Gering “have worked really close together to try to understand the number of ships it would require to achieve 3.0 based on current readiness,” Brodie noted.
“The two analytical arms of both services have come to the conclusion that it takes 40 ships. That’s 13 big decks and 27 LPDs,” the Maritime Expeditionary Warfare director explained.
Big decks are the Navy’s Wasp class (LHD) and America class (LHA) amphibious assault ships. Their embarked Aviation Combat Elements (ACEs) can include F-35B Joint Strike Fighters , MV-22 tiltrotor aircraft , UH-1 , AH-1 and CH-53 helicopters , as well as Navy Seahawk helicopters . The LPDs are smaller [ Amphibious Transport Dock ships ], which also embark MV-22s and helicopters.
The capabilities of MEUs have grown over the past decade, allowing them, in limited cases, to take on tasks that once required an aircraft carrier strike group. MV-22 tiltrotors, and, more recently, F-35Bs, which can be embarked in large numbers in the so-called “Lightning carrier” configuration, have boosted the utility of these fighting units.
The amphibious ship requirements, which had been in discussion for a while, were finally hammered out over the past few months by the new Amphibious Force Readiness Board (AFRB), stated Brodie. The AFRB is a joint Navy-Marine Corps effort created to better track the readiness of the amphibious fleet , which has been a huge issue as we have frequently noted .
“Right now, I have 31 amphibious warfare ships,” stated Brodie. The biggest need at the moment, he added, is for additional amphibious assault ships.
The law calls for the service to have 10, but currently it has only nine. That’s because the USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD-6) was sent to the scrapyard in 2021 after being ravaged by a fire in 2020 .
Brodie said the Marines want to increase the number of mandated amphibious assault ships from 10 to 13.
“When I have a problem generating this force, it really revolves around the big deck,” he stated.
The call for a fleet of 40 amphibious ships, and especially 13 big decks, is a sharp departure from the guidance former Commandant Gen. David Berger introduced in 2019 that led to his Force Design 2030 plan . In these documents, Berger called for fewer amphibious assault ships and more smaller vessels . Berger was concerned about the growing array of threats to these large, slow-moving vessels from anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, and that was before one-way attack drones became such ubiquitous weapons of war. This strategy was seen as better suited for fighting in the Pacific in a modern context, not large scale beach landings of the past.
He also wanted to return the Corps to its naval roots ; small, dispersed stand-in forces working inside an adversary’s weapons engagement zone after two decades of ground pounding in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Given how much of a sea-change this new plan represents, reaching a 40 amphibious ship fleet that includes 13 big decks is no small task.
“I’ve got a sheet sitting right here in front of me that tells me how we get there,” Brodie added. “You can’t get there tomorrow, right? The only way for me to realistically increase that inventory is for me to build new ships and do a service-life extension on some of the selective ships that I currently have in the inventory.”
Brodie said that Kilby and Gering are going to approach Congress later this month to convey the need for more ships.
There is no set timeline to reach the 40-ship goal, the Marines told TWZ .
“We will have to await future congressional funding for these,” Lt. Col. Eric D. Flanagan, a USMC spokesman, told us, adding that there is a multi-ship procurement contract underway for several amphibious vessels. He was referring to HII being awarded a $9.6 billion multi-ship procurement contract in 2024 for the construction of three San Antonio class amphibious ships and a contract modification for the next America class large-deck amphibious ship.
“This combined procurement — the first of its kind for amphibious ships — begins the journey for the construction of LPDs 33, 34, 35 and LHA 10 for the U.S. Navy,” HII stated at the time .
The request for additional shipbuilding funds will likely face far stiffer headwinds now that the Democrats have won control of both the Senate and the House.
While the Trump administration continues to pursue a roughly $1.5 trillion defense budget for Fiscal Year 2027, which includes some $350 billion that would come from outside normal defense spending streams via the reconciliation process , a letter leaked yesterday from a top Democrat offers a glimpse into the challenges the new amphibious ship plan may face.
The letter from Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington state Democrat who is in line to become chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, makes clear that many programs and policy issues, as well as defense spending writ large, are set to be put under the microscope when the Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote in his ‘dear colleagues’ letter.
All of this comes at a time when the Navy has been struggling to meet operational demands for surface combatants with its existing fleet. This has been further exacerbated by shakeups in separate plans to acquire new frigates and larger uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), as well as rising costs associated with its workhorse Arleigh Burke class destroyers .
On top of everything, conflicts in the Middle East have taken a toll on the Navy, incurring costs that need to be paid for.
In August, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle estimated as a result of the Operation Epic Fury fight against Iran, the Navy needed between $6 billion and $8 billion more than what was budgeted for in the 2026 fiscal year “to be whole and solvent for [Fiscal Year] 26,” Navy Times reported .
Overall, the U.S. military “has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July,” according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters last month .
In addition to not having enough ships to fulfill the mission, there is a big problem keeping the existing ones available. articles.title_orig: Memory Stocks Are Tanking. Should You Buy the Dip?
articles.title_zh: Memory Stocks Are Tanking. Should You Buy the Dip?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

Quantum computing stocks have spent the past month giving back ground, and IonQ ( NYSE:IONQ ) sits near the center of the slide. IonQ stock is down 32% over the past month, recently trading at $29.70. Shares are up 5% from the prior close, a modest bounce after a steep decline.
The selloff has hit the whole group, which suggests IonQ is moving with its sector as risk appetite for speculative technology cools off. Rigetti Computing ( NASDAQ:RGTI ) stock is down 28% over the past month to $10.94. Meanwhile, D-Wave Quantum ( NASDAQ:QBTS ) shares have slid 35% over the past month to $10.23, a steeper fall than IonQ's.
For IonQ, the pullback has come even after a strong second quarter and a string of acquisitions, leaving investors to figure out whether the slide points to lasting problems at IonQ or a correction across the whole sector.
IonQ's Q2 2026 revenue rose 287% year over year to a record $80.1 million in results released on August 5. Excluding acquisitions, IonQ grew 132% organically. CEO Niccolo de Masi spoke on the earnings call. He said that "Q2 2026 is the strongest quarter in IonQ's history and our fifth consecutive quarter of record results."

Management's 2026 revenue outlook for IonQ now includes the SkyWater Technology acquisition, which closed July 31, and calls for $450 million to $460 million. That $1.8 billion deal brought a semiconductor foundry in-house. On the hardware side, IonQ is developing its 256-qubit Superion system, and management plans to start commissioning those systems in 2027.
In September, IonQ announced a quantum computing partnership with NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ). A pending acquisition of Elisity would add to IonQ's quantum security business.
Wall Street remains mostly bullish on IonQ, with 11 Buy ratings and one Hold over the past three months. The average analyst price target on IonQ stands at $65.45.
IonQ's Q2 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) came in at negative $120.3 million, and its operating expenses reached $417.3 million. Under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), IonQ's net loss hit $1.9 billion, mostly because of a $1.6 billion non-cash warrant revaluation the company disclosed.
All the acquisitions make IonQ's organic growth harder to judge. Folding in SkyWater could also put pressure on IonQ's margins. On the August call, IonQ CFO Inder Singh said, "So don't draw a straight line up into the right from any one of the data points."
The commercial return for IonQ still depends on how well it executes and how fast customers adopt quantum tools. Quantum stocks have also been volatile. As the past month's drops at Rigetti and D-Wave show, that volatility is exactly why speculative names like these belong in a small, rules-based allocation of a portfolio (we laid out the sizing and exit rules in a free guide here).
IonQ builds trapped-ion quantum computers and sells a full platform covering computing, networking, sensing and security, while Rigetti uses superconducting qubits at a smaller scale and D-Wave works on quantum annealing, which suits a different class of problems.
With SkyWater and Nexus Photonics, IonQ now handles chip manufacturing and integrated photonics itself, a vertically integrated model its two peers don't share.
Q3 2026 results from IonQ arrive on November 5, after the market close. Analysts expect a loss of $0.34 per share, compared with a $3.58 loss a year earlier. Investors will be watching whether organic revenue keeps growing apart from acquired sales and whether SkyWater weighs on margins.
Bulls have record revenue, a bigger outlook and an active hardware roadmap on their side. IonQ's bears point to deep losses, heavy spending and a sector subject to sharp swings. Whether IonQ looks hopeless or ready for a rebound depends on which of those lists the coming quarters back up.
Investors can watch for updates on the Superion timeline and on SkyWater's margins in the upcoming report. Cautious traders may want to see how the debate over IonQ's margins settles before drawing any firm conclusions.
